checkpoints: Controlled: the field's value lives in React state; every onChange calls setState → re-renders both the form root component and the sibling fields on EVERY keystroke — that cost grows with the number of fields, so bigger forms get slower.
Uncontrolled (RHF): register("email") just stores a ref pointing at the DOM node; the BROWSER owns the value, RHF only reads it when needed (when handleSubmit or getValues runs).

Because no state changes while typing, rendering is decoupled entirely from each keystroke — that is why RHF is markedly faster on 30+ field forms: the engine only subscribes to the DOM via refs and re-renders when actually necessary, not because it is "tidier syntax" as the shallow reading assumes.

Trade-off: since RHF does not itself know a value changed, derived state (disabling a button based on a field, a live preview, cross-field validation) does not update on its own — you must subscribe explicitly with watch/useWatch in the exact component that needs the value.
useWatch re-renders only its caller, so you keep the uncontrolled model's performance benefit, and you avoid calling watch() for the whole form at the root since that widens the re-render scope.
Bonus depth: formState is itself a proxy — reading isSubmitting directly in JSX already subscribes that key for re-render, with no need to declare a separate loading useState.

Debounce resets a timer on every new event; only once events STOP for X ms does the action actually fire — meaning you only ask the server about the FINAL value ("zora42"), never the intermediate characters (pure noise, asking about them would be meaningless).

Throttle is the opposite: it fires at a fixed maximum rate WHILE events keep streaming — right for a signal you need to track continuously, like scroll position or mouse movement, but completely wrong for a username check, because there the intermediate values are noise, not a signal worth tracking.

On window size: this is a UX-versus-network trade-off — 300ms feels snappy but coalesces fewer requests (a fast typer can still cross that window multiple times), while 800ms and up starts to feel laggy, making the user wait too long to see feedback; 500ms is the commonly-used sweet spot.

The most commonly misunderstood point: debounce only solves ONE of two independent axes — it cuts the COUNT of requests (coalescing 6 keystrokes into 1 call about the final value), but it does NOT guarantee the ORDERING of the responses that come back.

If the user pauses, types more, then pauses again quickly, two requests can still be in flight on the network at once, and because latency varies, the response of the OLDER request can still arrive AFTER the response of the NEWER request and overwrite the fresh state with stale data — that's a separate race condition.

That race condition requires a separate mechanism (cancelling the request with AbortController, or attaching a stale guard that compares against the current value) to fix; debounce alone is not enough.
Two real defects, different in nature — one is an error mis-addressed to the wrong place, the other is state actually being corrupted — and both must be fixed before approving.

Finding 1 + fix: .refine attaches its issue wherever path points; here path isn't declared, so the issue falls straight to the form ROOT while the component only reads errors.items — the error genuinely exists (submit still fails, matching QA's "silently blocked" report) but the UI never finds it where it's looking; fix by adding path: ['items'] to the .refine so the error lands under the items key, where the row list is rendered.

Finding 1b — even with the right path, the RHF v7 resolver shim may store the message at errors.items.root.message (root wrapping the child object) or at errors.items.message depending on version — so it must be rendered with errors.items?.root?.message ?? errors.items?.message to be safe across versions.

At the same time, keep the three validation tiers distinct: per-row errors at errors.items[index].field (by index), cardinality from array().min(1), and the aggregate from .refine — three different addresses that must never be conflated.

Finding 2 + fix: fields.reverse() reorders the fields object returned by useFieldArray without going through any of the hook's own API — the field.id ↔ value map and the items.N path rebinding are only maintained by append/remove/move/swap, so mutating outside that bookkeeping lets values drift away from their real entry, producing exactly the "values mix across rows" QA reported; fix by dropping fields.reverse() + setValue entirely and permuting via move/swap instead (or dropping the Reverse feature) — never mutate fields directly.
Required test 1: submitting a zero-total invoice → assert the items-error element shows the right message and that no POST /invoices request leaves.
Required test 2: reordering two rows via the new button → assert values travel with their real entry (desc-0 becomes "B", desc-1 becomes "A").
Required test 3: a row with invalid input (e.g. an empty description) still renders its own field error, proving the three validation tiers don't step on each other.

Run the Zod schema validation (regex + length) first, synchronously and free of network cost, before ever scheduling the debounce timer — so structurally invalid values like `ad`, `XYZ`, `zora 4` never leave the browser

Guard against the effect firing on mount for a profile form whose `defaultValues` prefill the current username, by skipping the check while the field is pristine (`formState.isDirty === false` or an explicit pristine flag) so a prefilled default produces zero requests until the user actually types

Dedupe identical values against a round-trip by keying past verdicts by the username string, so retyping the same value answers from cache instead of re-querying — e.g. TanStack Query's `['check-username', username]` queryKey gets this for free
Fix the lying error state: the `catch` branch must set `idle` (never `taken`), because a 5xx or network failure is a server problem, not evidence the username is unavailable

Leave the 500ms debounce itself untouched, since it solves a separate axis (coalescing a burst of keystrokes into one request) and the UX invariant must hold — a structurally-valid value the user is actively typing still resolves to a verdict exactly one debounce-window after they stop

Verify the win with request-count assertions: invalid input → 0 requests; prefilled mount → 0 requests; retyping the same value → served from cache with request count unchanged; simulated 500 → `idle`, not `taken`
The inputs themselves are not the bug: `description` via `register` and `quantity`/`unitPrice` via `Controller` + `NumberField` are already uncontrolled, and rows are correctly keyed by `field.id`

Root cause is `watch("items")` called at the root of `DynamicFieldsClient`, which re-subscribes the root component to the entire items array so any keystroke in any one of the ~100 rows re-renders the root and its whole subtree, including every `LineItemRow`

State the general principle: `watch`/`useWatch` subscriptions are scoped to the calling component, not to the data they read, so placing the subscription at the root over the whole array maximizes the blast radius

Fix by pushing derived values down to where they're needed: a small `RowSubtotal` component calls `useWatch({ control, name: `items.${index}` })` for its own row only, so typing in row N re-renders exactly that one subscriber

Round out the fix: isolate the grand-total computation into its own component that subscribes to `items` independently, and keep the row list itself rendering off `fields` from `useFieldArray` (which only changes on append/remove/move) so the list was never part of the keystroke-driven render path to begin with

Note that wrapping `LineItemRow` in `React.memo` alone would not fix this, since the root's `watch` + `reduce` still re-run and still recreate the `subtotal` prop on every keystroke — the wide subscription must be deleted, not just insulated against
Identify the next lever if row count keeps growing as virtualization — rendering only viewport rows, since the bottleneck then shifts from render scope to raw row count

Verify the fix with the Profiler/render counters (before: the whole list repaints per keystroke; after: only the touched row's subtotal does), plus a functional check that subtotals and grand total still track edits, appends, and removals correctly
Define the component's API contract as `DynamicListField<TForm>` taking `{ control, name, renderRow, makeNewRow, minRows = 1, maxRows? }`

Internally call `useFieldArray({ control, name })` and own the `fields.map` keyed by `field.id` entirely inside the component, so that detail never leaks to the consumer and an index-key bug becomes impossible to reintroduce
Give `renderRow` the row `index` plus `register`/`control` so the consumer draws a row's own content and binds the positional path (`items.${index}.field`) without ever touching the key

Expose mutations only as semantic callbacks — `onAdd` calls `append(makeNewRow())`, `onRemove(i)` calls `remove(i)`, `onMoveUp`/`onMoveDown` call `move(i, i∓1)` — with `isDisabled` flags precomputed at the `minRows`/`maxRows` boundaries
Never return the raw `fields` array to the consumer, so a hand-mutation like `fields.reverse()` is impossible by construction, not merely discouraged by convention

Keep validation schema-side: per-row rules live in the item's schema and render inside each row, while the aggregate `array().min(1)` plus `.refine({ path: [name] })` belongs to the consumer's form schema, with the component only reserving a slot that defensively renders `root.message ?? message`

Defend the design: this API removes exactly the two recurring bug families (index keys, hand mutations) while the render-prop preserves layout freedom and schema-side validation keeps one source of truth — the component is a state-and-mutation shell, not a validator
Defines a data-driven step descriptor (e.g. `{ id, fields, component, enabled(values) }`) and turns the step list into an ordered registry of these descriptors, replacing the hard-coded if/else chain

Derives the active step list on every render by filtering the registry against the live form values (e.g. `registry.filter(s => s.enabled(values))`), so the tax-id step's presence follows the account-type answer instead of being hardcoded

Rewrites `goNext`/`Back` to work generically over the active list — validate only the current active step's fields, then move to the next/previous entry in that list — instead of branching per step index
Renders the progress indicator from the active list (e.g. `active.map(id)`) instead of a fixed-length array of steps

Models the schema branch with a discriminated union (or an equivalent root-level conditional refinement) keyed on the branching field, so the final parse validates whichever branch the user actually took, while shared cross-step rules still run via a root `.refine()`

Tracks the wizard's current position by the step's stable ID rather than a numeric index, and re-clamps to the nearest still-active step whenever the active list recomputes after the user flips the branching answer
Keeps the abandoned branch's data out of the final submitted payload — excluded by the union shape itself, or explicitly reset when its step drops out of the active list

Keeps the wizard a single mounted form (one `useForm`/`FormProvider` instance with `defaultValues` covering every branch's fields) with inactive steps hidden via `display: none` rather than unmounted, so Back never loses previously entered values

Set `mode: 'onBlur'` for this signup form, since it validates a field the moment it loses focus — judging a finished value rather than a half-typed one — which satisfies both the per-field-feedback request and the not-on-first-keystroke warning
Explain that the current setup has no `mode` set at all, which RHF defaults to `onSubmit`, and that's exactly why nothing shows until Submit dumps every field's errors at once

Argue `onChange` is wrong as a global default here because it fires on every keystroke (the hostile behavior the PM flagged), but is the right choice for a field that wants genuinely live per-character feedback, such as a password-strength meter or a slug/availability check

Flag that after the first submit, RHF switches re-validation behavior via `reValidateMode` (which defaults to `onChange`), so once an error has been seen it updates on every keystroke instead of waiting for blur — and that this asymmetry is deliberate, fixable with an explicit `reValidateMode: 'onBlur'` if the PM wants uniform cadence

State the underlying mechanism is unchanged across all modes: whichever trigger fires, RHF calls the `zodResolver` pipeline, which parses values and pushes issues into `formState.errors`, and `FieldError` just renders whatever is there — changing `mode`/`reValidateMode` only changes WHEN validation runs, never what it produces
Two things must survive reload, not one: values and position.
For values — since FormProvider shares exactly ONE useForm instance, methods.getValues() returns the entire { account, profile, preferences } shape at any point in time.
Persist by serializing that whole object into localStorage (e.g. on every step change) — a single snapshot covers all 3 steps, no per-step bookkeeping needed.
Restore with methods.reset(JSON.parse(stored)) to reload the values back.
For position — keep the step index in the URL as ?step=1, so reload (and sharing/bookmarking the link) reopens exactly where the user left off, instead of always dropping back to step 0.

The trap is the TIMING of the restore: seeding useForm's defaultValues straight from localStorage.getItem(...) makes the very first render depend on storage — a value flash right now — and if SSR is ever bolted on later, this same timing produces a genuine hydration mismatch: the server always renders empty because it has no localStorage, the client renders the stored value, React sees the two trees disagree.

The correct pattern: mount with the normal empty defaultValues, then restore AFTER mount inside useEffect(() => methods.reset(stored), []) — accepting one empty-then-restored flash instead of a mismatch that's much harder to debug.

Lifecycle hygiene: wipe the stored snapshot from localStorage right after a successful final POST, and if someone deep-links straight into a high ?step=, still re-run validation/gating before honoring that position — a URL query param is not a trusted source of truth on its own.
Keeping the interface plus a hand-written validate function isn't leaner — it's TWO declarations of the same truth, and every rule change is a chance for them to drift.

Root cause: an interface only exists at compile time — once the build finishes it's gone, so it can never validate anything at runtime on its own; the hand-written validate function must be a SECOND, separate declaration copying the same rules.

A Zod schema is different: it's an object that lives at runtime, where each chained method (.string(), .email(), .min(8)) both registers a check that runs immediately AND carries the exact structure z.infer<typeof schema> reads to derive the compile-time type — one declaration does both jobs, so there is no second copy left to drift; e.g. adding .regex(/[A-Z]/) to the password rule updates both the validator and the type in exactly one line.
Plugged into useForm via zodResolver, schema.safeParse(values) runs and — per React Hook Form's resolver contract — ALWAYS returns { values, errors }, never throws.

A passing parse leaves errors empty and handleSubmit calls onValid with already-typed data; a failing parse maps the ZodIssue array into errors BY FIELD PATH (errors.email, errors.password) — and because safeParse collects every issue before returning (no fail-fast), submitting an empty form pops EVERY field's error at once instead of stopping at the first one.

Contrast: a hand-written resolver that throws instead of returning { values, errors } would collapse every error to form-level, losing all per-field detail — the resolver contract itself is what makes per-field errors possible.

The boundary: the schema is a local, synchronous gate — a rule like "does this email already exist" needs a round-trip to the server, so it cannot live in the sync schema and must live in a separate async mechanism (e.g. an async refinement, or a server-side check) outside that local syntax gate.
